item.title: REVIEW: Vivint Outdoor Camera Pro 3 Review: A Solid Upgrade for Vivint Homes Only
item.description:
Source: PCMag
When I reviewed Vivint’s $399.99 Outdoor Camera Pro Gen 2 back in 2022, I liked its crisp image quality, onboard video storage, and Smart Deter feature, but wasn't so pleased with its high price, lack of third-party device support, and reliance on an existing Vivint security system. The Outdoor Camera Pro 3 offers an upgraded image sensor and AI-powered radar motion detection, but at $399.99, it’s still expensive and only works with a Vivint home security system. It’s a good choice for Vivint users, but if you’re looking for an outdoor camera that works with third-party platforms and offers mechanical pan and tilt, the $219.99 Reolink Altas PT Ultra is our Editors' Choice. The Outdoor Camera Pro 3 has a white IP65 weather-resistant camera housing measuring 3.2 by 3.2 by 1.3 inches (HWD). A swivel arm connects the camera housing to a base that contains an 85dB speaker and a port for connecting an optional $249.99 Spotlight Pro fixture. Around the back is a cable that connects to a Power over Ethernet (PoE) adapter. As with the Gen 2 model, this camera uses PoE and a Wi-Fi bridge to connect to your home network and to the Vivint smart hub. Like other Vivint cameras, it only works with a Vivint home security system and doesn't support Alexa, Google, HomeKit, or IFTTT. The front of the camera is black and holds the lens, a laser light ring, four infrared LEDs for black-and-white night vision, two microphones, and a radar sensor. The light ring briefly glows green when the camera is connected to the hub, shines blue when two-way talk is active, and is red when the Smart Sentry or siren is triggered. Vivint’s radar technology measures movement and distance and uses AI to distinguish motion from humans, animals, passing cars, and wind-blown objects. It’ll let you know if someone is lurking on your property or near your car and will trigger Smart Deter, which sounds a siren and illuminates the LED ring to let intruders know they are being watched. When paired with the Vivint Spotlight Pro, the camera will activate the spotlight and track whoever is on your property. Like the Outdoor Camera Pro Gen 2, the Pro 3 uses a 4K HDR image sensor but, oddly, only provides 1080p streaming and recorded video. It has a 140-degree field of view, and the upgraded image sensor offers 5.3x HD zoom and 10x digital zoom, whereas the Gen 2 sensor offers 3x HD zoom and 10x digital zoom. For comparison, the Reolink Altas PT Ultra captures true 4K video with a 90-degree field of view and supports 90 degrees of vertical tilt and 355 degrees of horizontal panning. The Outdoor Pro 3 will record motion events and store the video on both an internal 64GB SD card and in the cloud. The Reolink Altas PT Ultra works with microSD cards up to 512GB (sold separately), and doesn't support cloud storage. You can control the Outdoor Camera Pro 3 and access recorded video using the Vivint mobile app for iOS and Android devices, the same app that pairs with your Vivint security system. It appears on the My Home screen under Cameras, in a panel that displays the camera's name and its most recent captured image. Tap the panel to view a live stream you can watch in full-screen mode by turning your phone sideways. Below the video panel are buttons for rewinding the video, locking and unlocking any installed locks, enabling two-way talk, taking a snapshot, and enabling the spotlight. At the very bottom of the screen is an Events button that opens a screen with a list of thumbnails for all camera events. Tap any thumbnail to play the clip or share it with other users. At the top of the screen is a button to enable or disable the Smart Deter feature. Back on the camera’s My Home panel, three dots in the upper-right corner take you to a settings screen. Here you can configure notifications and recording modes and create detection zones. Use the Deter Mode option to enable Smart Deter for people who linger and/or get too close to your car. Other settings let you create rules for the spotlight to follow people, the lights to turn on at a specific time, night vision to turn on or off, or to enable or disable each of the nine spotlight beams. Within settings, you can also configure the siren and video quality. At the bottom of the My Home screen are My Home, Activity, Shop, and For You buttons. The My Home button takes you back to the My Home screen from anywhere in the app, and the Activity button opens a screen listing all system events, including video clips. The Shop button takes you to a screen where you can purchase additional Vivint devices, and the For You button provides access to device and account information. The Outdoor Camera Pro 3 requires professional installation just like every other Vivint outdoor cam. As always, the Vivint technician was prompt and polite and needed just under one hour to install the camera, attach the Spotlight Pro fixture, and pair the camera to my Vivint hub. The Outdoor Camera Pro 3 worked well in testing. Daytime video appeared crisp with well-saturated colors, and black-and-white night video showed good contrast and sharp image detail. The camera’s radar motion detection worked as intended, sending alerts and activating Smart Deter whenever there was lingering motion in my driveway near my cars. Motion events were correctly identified and arrived swiftly. The siren was loud, and the LED ring did a good job of letting visitors know that they were being observed. Integrations with other Vivint components worked well. I created a Smart Action to have my side door unlock when the camera detected motion, and it worked without issue, as did my Smart Action to have the camera start recording when my back door was opened. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. If you currently own a Vivint home security system, adding the Vivint Outdoor Camera Pro 3 is a smart choice for monitoring activities on and around your property, but at $399.99, it sits at the high end of the price spectrum for an outdoor security camera. Video is sharp, but despite being touted as a 4K camera, it maxes out at 1080p. If you're not already in Vivint's ecosystem, our Editors’ Choice winner, the Reolink Altas PT Ultra, is nearly half the price and offers true 4K video, mechanical pan and tilt, and interoperability with third-party smart home ecosystems. I’ve been working with computers for ages, starting with a multi-year stint in purchasing for a major IBM reseller in New York City before eventually landing at PCMag (back when it was still in print as PC Magazine). I spent more than 14 years on staff, most recently as the director of operations for PC Labs, before hitting the freelance circuit as a contributing editor.

item.title: REVIEW: UPERFECT GR14BU portable monitor review: A 120 Hz 3K OLED touch display at a killer price
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
Although it has some flaws, the GR14BU excels in value pricing, features, and performance. - -Kickstand and overall design don’t support portrait mode Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. As the portable monitor category matures, a number of new players have entered the market to claim their share of the pie. One company that we haven’t had a chance to sample yet is UPERFECT. But the company is coming out of the gate swinging with the first review sample that it sent our way: the GR14BU. As its name suggests, the GR14BU is a 14-inch portable monitor, but it doesn’t have a run-of-the-mill 60 Hz 1080p IPS panel like you’ll find on most of the best portable monitors in this segment. Instead, it features an OLED panel with a dense 2880 × 1800 (3K) resolution and a 120 Hz maximum refresh rate. On top of that, the GR14BU also supports touch input in Windows 11. On paper, it’s a promising product with a street price of under $300. That’s roughly three times the price of a garden-variety 14-inch IPS panels, but is it worth the premium? At first glance, the GR14BU impresses with its black aluminum frame that wraps around the 14-inch panel. The sleek design is enhanced by the glossy glass, which is typical for OLED panels. Things take a downward turn from there, however. While the GR14BU features an integrated kickstand, which is much appreciated on a portable monitor, it’s tiny and is mounted directly in the middle of the back panel of the monitor. Because of this position, the GR14BU can only be used in landscape mode. Even if you could somehow prop the monitor up in portrait mode, this would be hindered by the two USB-C ports and HDMI port on the right side of the monitor, and the five OSD buttons on the left side. Speaking of the OSD buttons, they feel cheap and wobble around like buttons you might find on a cheap plastic stopwatch you’d find at Dollar Tree. They’re shockingly bad for a device with a $399 MSRP. The five buttons are: Power, OSD, Up, Down, and Back. UPERFECT included a plethora of cables and adapters in the box, which should satisfy all your connectivity needs. Our review unit included two USB-C-to-USB-C cables, one micro-HDMI to HDMI cable, two 180-degree USB-C to USB-C adapters, one 180-degree micro-HDMI to HDMI adapter, and one USB-C wall adapter. One thing to note as we discuss cables and adapters is that when connecting the GR14BU to my test system using a single USB-C to USB-C cable, the monitor was locked at 20 percent brightness and would not go any higher. However, when using the second USB-C to USB-C adapter connected to the USB-C wall adapter, the GR14BU would automatically boost brightness to its maximum level. The OSD on the GR14BU is no-frills, offering just the basic controls that you’d expect to find on a portable monitor. Without even accessing the main OSD, pressing the Up button brings up the volume controls, with a subsequent press of the Up button raising the volume, while pressing the Down button lowers the volume. Likewise, pressing the Down button separately invokes the Brightness menu. Pressing the dedicated OSD button brings up the full menu, where you can access picture and color settings. Pressing the Up and Down buttons navigates you through the OSD; pressing the OSD button again executes a menu item, while the Back button takes you back one level in the OSD. Display Performance on the UPERFECT GR14BU The GR14BU features a 14-inch display with a dense-for-its-size 2880 x 1600 resolution, in a 16:10 aspect ratio. That pixel-dense panel is backed by a 120 Hz refresh rate, which is twice that of most portable monitors, along with multi-touch support in Windows 11. UPERFECT claims that the GR14BU has a maximum brightness of 500 nits, but we measured a maximum of 368.6 nits when plugged in at 100 percent. While well short of the manufacturer’s claim, this is clsoe to peers like the Asus ZenScreen OLED MQ16AH (369.4 nits) and ViewSonic ColorPro VP16-OLED (369.8 nits). Our instrumented tests also showed similar color performance to the Asus and ViewSonic. The GR14BU measured 132.2 percent coverage of the DCI-P3 color space, while sRGB coverage came in at 186.6 percent. In real-world scenarios, I found the panel to be sufficiently bright in my well-lit home office, and even enough to overcome most reflections when sitting outside in overcast conditions. Colors looked vibrant, with especially punchy reds and greens while looking at nature footage on YouTube. As with all OLED monitors, black levels were impeccable, which I particularly took note of while watching the latest teaser trailers for Avengers: Doomsday. For my usual productivity tasks, I was really disappointed that I couldn’t use the GR14BU in portrait mode, which is probably the biggest miss for me. I like having that versatility to switch between portrait and landscape modes at will. I also tested out the 120 Hz refresh rate at native resolution for gaming. I played Battlefield 6 with the GR14BU hooked up to my desktop computer via HDMI and had no trouble until there was heavy action on the screen. It was then that frame rates momentarily dipped into the 90 fps range, and I noticed a bit of screen tearing. The GR14BU doesn’t support any kind of Adaptive-Sync technology, like FreeSync or G-Sync. UPERFECT includes a pair of tinny speakers integrated into the GR14BU. There is quite a bit of audio distortion once you get past 75 percent, but if you keep the volume at a moderate level, the quality is passable. There’s no bass, and music sounds flat (I tried various genres, ranging from Jay-Z to Susanne Sundfør to Jai Wolf). You’re better off relying on your laptop’s built-in speakers than relying on the pair included on the GR14BU. I came in expecting a lot from the UPERFECT GR14BU, given its specs. However, there are plenty of caveats. The GR14BU has a bright and colorful 3K OLED panel, along with a 120 Hz refresh rate. It even includes an integrated kickstand and internal speakers. However, the kickstand doesn’t allow the monitor to be used in portrait mode, and the 120 Hz maximum refresh rate doesn’t have the backing of Adaptive-Sync. There are also some quality lapses, like the woefully cheap OSD buttons. However, much of this can be overlooked considering the price. The GR14BU can be had right now for $299 from Amazon, making it an incredible value given the specs. For comparison, we recently reviewed the Asus ZenScreen OLED (MQ16FC), which has a 16.1-inch 1200p OLED non-touch display with a 60 Hz refresh rate. The GR14BU outclasses the MQ16FC in color performance, brightness, and specs while only commanding a $30 premium and including touch. That’s an impressive feat, despite its design and build deficiencies.

item.title: REVIEW: Apple iMac (2026) Review: New M6 Muscle, Same Timeless All-in-One
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Like the steady ticking of clockwork, it's time for a new iMac, Apple's iconic all-in-one (AIO) computer. Without a hardware update since 2024's M4-powered model, the 24-inch iMac was due for an upgrade, and it has arrived with the new M6-powered iMac (starts at $1,499; $1,899 as tested). New features and capabilities come with the addition of M6 Apple silicon, but don't get your hopes up for a major redesign. This is very nearly an exact copy of the iMac design we've seen in recent years, from the 24-inch display to the snazzy color-matched peripherals. Still, even with the M6 chip being the only noteworthy improvement, the iMac continues to earn its Editors' Choice award as the best (and only) Mac AIO you can buy. The 2026 iMac offers two different M6 processor options. The base model comes with a 10-core CPU, a 10-core GPU, and a 16-core Neural Engine. It's got a pair of USB Type-C/Thunderbolt 4 ports, 16GB of memory, and a 256GB SSD. The higher-end configuration comes with two additional USB-C/Thunderbolt 4 ports and a beefier M6 chip, with a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU (though it keeps the same Neural Engine). It starts at $1,699. Our review unit has the default 16GB of unified memory, but you can step up to 24GB or 32GB, sold in $200 increments. Our review unit also comes with an upgraded 512GB SSD for $200. All told, our system rings up at $1,899. If you want even more storage, you can select 1TB or 2TB options, although the prices climb quickly, with the 2TB SSD adding a full $1,000 to the sticker price. The standard display finish is glossy, but for an extra $200, you can instead opt for "nano-texture" glass, which uses micro-faceting across the surface to reduce reflections and glare. This upgrade is available only for the 12-core, four-port model. All told, the most expensive version of the iMac (excluding any upgrades to peripherals or software) sells for $2,899. All models come with a keyboard and mouse. Finally, you can add AppleCare+ and AppleCare One extended coverage, which provides unlimited repairs for accidents such as drops and spills, 24/7 expert support, and certified repairs with authorized parts. AppleCare+ is $6.99 per month, or $69.99 per year. If you want to cover multiple products, AppleCare One ($19.99 per month) allows you to cover up to three devices and adds theft and loss coverage for smaller items like the iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch. Students and teachers also enjoy small but exclusive discounts: $50 off the base model, and $100 off higher-priced configurations. As in years past, the biggest, most visible feature on the iMac is a 23.5-inch display with a resolution of 4,480 by 2,520 pixels. It's a top-notch screen, and I'll discuss its quality in more detail below. Touch screens have finally arrived on the MacBook, but not on the iMac. Instead, your primary inputs will be the included Magic Keyboard and Magic Mouse, both hued to match the anodized finish of the iMac's aluminum body. They match whichever color you chose for the iMac itself: blue, purple, pink, orange, yellow, green, or silver. (I like that Apple doesn't make you guess about what obscure names of specific tints and hues look like, as it does with some of its other products.) Even the included power and USB-C cables to charge the peripherals are color-matched. We tested the blue iMac shown in the photos here. I find that under certain lighting conditions, the blue anodized metal looks more silver. The overall design of the iMac is elegantly spare, but you almost have to appreciate the simplicity. The integrated stand allows you to adjust the screen angle, but not height. If you want that sort of flexibility, you will need to configure your iMac with the optional VESA mount, which bolts on an H-shaped bracket right where the hinge otherwise attaches, allowing you to mount it on a standard wall mount or adjustable arm. The VESA mount adapter option does not change the price of the iMac, but it does mean you'll have to bring your own compatible mount. The L-shaped stand is milled from solid aluminum and is pleasantly sturdy. As ever, the included peripherals will be good enough for many users, but an acquired taste if you are picky about keyboard comfort and ergonomics. The Magic Keyboard with Touch ID is included in the purchase price of the iMac, while an extra $30 will get you the Magic Keyboard with Touch ID and Numeric Keypad, which adds a full number pad as well as a less cramped arrow cluster and some additional function keys. The Apple Magic Mouse is also included in the iMac's base price. If you'd like, an extra $50 will let you upgrade to the Magic Trackpad; both are Multi-Touch surfaces that support gestures such as swiping and scrolling, while the trackpad also has Apple's Force Touch contextual menu technology. If you're upgrading from a pre-2024 iMac, you'll appreciate that the peripherals now have USB-C charging ports rather than Lightning ports. The integrated 12-megapixel Center Stage camera is just as great as it was in 2024, with the neat trick of capturing not only forward-facing images for video meetings, but also a desktop view that's great for showing objects and documents or demonstrating a manual process. It still only captures 1080p video; my hopes for a 4K or even 1440p camera were dashed. One of my favorite things about the iMac is how cleanly it handles connectivity. The connector for the power cable has a magnetic unidirectional plug, so you won't have to fumble with aligning pins or anything like that when plugging it in. And the four USB-C Thunderbolt 4 ports on the back of the iMac are capable and highly adaptable, thanks to the high data throughput and universally compatible USB-C interface. A 3.5mm audio jack is on the left-hand corner of the slim chassis. You can use Bluetooth 6 for wireless headphones and peripherals, while Wi-Fi 7 handles the networking. The only clunky connection on the iMac isn't even on the all-in-one desktop itself but is instead relegated to the power brick. That is where you will find the Ethernet port. As for adding additional monitors, since all four of the USB-C Thunderbolt 4 ports support DisplayPort output, you can connect a compatible monitor to any of them, but not all four at once. The 12-core model supports up to two external monitors (at either 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz), and you could even connect the two displays in a daisy-chain configuration through a single Thunderbolt port. However, if you want higher resolution or refresh rates (8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz, or 4K/240Hz), you're limited to a single external monitor. The M6 chip is the big upgrade coming to the new iMac. It's Apple's first true 2-nanometer processor, progressing beyond the "3nm Class" designation that was used across the M5 generation. It also introduces a new three-tier core hierarchy to the processor. The 12-core CPU has two Super cores (the max-frequency cores dedicated to peak single-thread performance), four Performance cores (which do the traditional heavy lifting for multi-threaded sustained compute), and six Efficiency cores (which use far less power and are better suited to background processes). You'll see how the M6 fares in our benchmarks below, but the fact is that it is a substantial upgrade over the M4 processor used in the 2024 iMac. If you were hoping for an external redesign, perhaps the M6 will lessen your disappointment. The higher core count and more capable cores deliver faster, more responsive performance across the board, but that's not the full extent of improvements the new chip promises. Gaming and creative apps in particular get a boost because Apple has improved the graphics performance of the 12-core GPU by integrating neural acceleration hardware into every GPU core. These additional accelerators speed up AI workloads, but are especially well-suited to image processing tasks, and are distinct from conventional game rendering. The chip is also built for multitasking, and macOS 27 Golden Gate takes advantage of this in several ways. Visual refinements to the translucent Liquid Glass interface improve the overall design, with a cleaner look and sharper border contrast. Scheduler optimizations in macOS 27 mean lightweight and persistent tasks go to the efficiency cores and neural accelerator, freeing up Super cores for heavier demands. Among other things, they can ensure the visual experience is silky smooth: no stuttering window movement or jerky video playback here. The new processor adds support for Siri AI and Image Playground if you opt for the dual 16-core Neural Engine (that's 32 total Neural Engine cores, as well as GPU cores with additional neural accelerators built into every graphics core). The processor will even support smaller open-weight AI models, but with only 16GB of unified memory, this is not the Mac for local AI. You can read more about the software in our full review of macOS 27, linked above. To quantify and compare the iMac's performance, we've gathered four comparison systems, starting with the previous iMac. The Apple iMac (2024, M4) uses Apple's 3-nanometer-class M4 chip, which has a 10-core design and only a single 16-core Neural Engine. If you're wondering about upgrading from an earlier iMac, this is the comparison to watch most closely. We're also comparing the M6 iMac to the Apple Mac mini (2026, M6). Both machines run on the same 12-core M6 chip, but have quite different thermal dissipation and airflow due to their radically different designs. They also have different value propositions, since the Mac mini is available at a lower price but requires you to provide your own monitor and peripherals. To see how the M6 stacks up against the M5 Pro, we've also included the other Apple Mac mini released this year (the 2026 M5 Pro version), so you can get a clear idea of how the two processor options compare. For Windows and x86 systems, we look at the Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini, which represents the current standard in compact Windows desktop computing. We're also including one of our top-rated Windows AIOs, and a direct competitor to the iMac on price, the Dell 24 All-in-One (2026). The Dell's 1080p display is far beneath the iMac's splendid screen, so the Dell 24 is more of a mainstream value competitor. Because macOS does not support our usual PCMark tests, our productivity testing focuses instead on our CPU-centric benchmarks. First, Maxon's Cinebench 2024 renders a complex scene using the company's Cinema 4D engine. Next, Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning. Finally, we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. In these tests, the M6 iMac performs quite well, especially compared with the Dell 24 All-in-One. But it's not a leader in this batch of comparison systems. We see a solid improvement over the M4 iMac, demonstrating the progression from M4 to M6, but the Apple Mac mini offers even better scores with that same M6 hardware. And the leader of the pack is the Mac mini with M5 Pro, demonstrating that last-gen high-tier silicon remains your best bet for peak performance. That's more or less what we see in HandBrake as well, where the M6 iMac finishes our video transcoding test in just under 4 minutes. That's a solid improvement over the M4 model, but it falls short of every other Mac on the list. It is less than half the time to completion that the Dell 24-inch All-in-One required, though: a whopping 9 minutes on the same task. If you're working with video in any capacity, the iMac is the better choice. And in Geekbench Pro, where we look at both multi-core and single-core general productivity, the iMac comes in very close to the M6 Mac mini, with a healthy margin over the M4 iMac. The Mac mini with M5 Pro is still the leader of the pack, scoring significantly higher in multi-core tasking, but not in single-core performance. The Windows machines here aren't putting up a great fight, with lower scores across both multi- and single-core performance. Our graphics performance testing starts with four of UL's macOS-ready 3DMark benchmarks. Steel Nomad Light is a 1440p test without ray tracing, focusing on raw graphics rasterization, while Steel Nomad (no "Light" in its title) is more advanced. Solar Bay is where ray-tracing testing comes in, and the Wild Life Extreme test pushes Macs to their limits at 4K resolution. We also measure gaming performance using the 2022 strategy game Total War: Warhammer 3 via Steam, which we run exclusively on Macs. In the game's Battle benchmark, we run the test at Ultra and Low settings at 1080p resolution and record the average frames per second (fps). Finally, we've adapted our Cyberpunk 2077 test, which we run on Windows gaming PCs, to Macs. Our Cyberpunk 2077 test settings push systems to their limits without frame generation or resolution upscaling, using the Ultra and all-out Ray Tracing Overdrive graphics presets at 1080p and 1440p for desktop Macs, or 1200p and 1600p for MacBooks. I was very curious to see how the graphics performance would be on the iMac with this M6 and the added neural acceleration hardware in the graphics cores, but the difference wasn't as profound as I anticipated. The M5 Pro Mac mini still leads way out in front, thanks to its 20-core GPU. Then, the Mac mini M6 also puts up slightly better scores than the Apple iMac, despite having the same graphics hardware. This is likely due to the better airflow afforded by the bulkier mini PC design. But the iMac is still a force to be reckoned with when compared against these Windows desktops. It edges ahead of the Asus NUC by over 1,000 points and absolutely trounces the Dell 24 All-in-One with its basic integrated Intel Graphics. That's more or less the pattern across all of our 3DMark tests, whether we were focused on general graphics or ray tracing. The most interesting results were actually in gaming, which has traditionally been Apple's weak spot. Over the generations, as the GPU cores in different M-series systems have grown in number and in capability, results have improved. In this case, we're seeing fairly impressive performance in Total War: Warhammer 3, staying well into the playable range, even at higher resolution settings. But the real test is an AAA title, such as Cyberpunk 2077. And in this case, we see playable results—a notable improvement all on its own. We could run the game at the higher resolution and with ray tracing, tests that the previous iMac wasn't even able to complete. The gaming performance is still fairly modest, but it's now at a place where we can recommend the iMac for people who want some gaming capability. You'll just need to remember to keep the resolution and eye-candy settings at modest levels to attain those playable frame rates. We also use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). As I mentioned earlier, the display on the iMac is just as great as it has been in years past, offering 100% sRGB color coverage and scoring quite well in the Adobe RGB and DCI-P3 color spaces. That makes sense since it is unchanged from the already impressive display on last year's iMac. If you liked the display on that older model, you'll still like it now. Most important, it delivers better performance and higher resolution than the 1080p 24-inch display on the Dell 24 All-in-One. Apple iMac (2026, M6) - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. If you want a zero-friction Mac that's far more spacious than a MacBook, the iMac is an obvious choice. But is it the best value? In terms of the complete setup, absolutely, since you'll get a spectacular 4.5K Retina display, color-matched keyboard and mouse, and great capability for everyday computing. It's our Editors’ Choice-winning Mac AIO for a reason. But if you want to save a few bucks or get more processing power, you'd want the Mac mini, which is substantially cheaper and can be outfitted with the more powerful M5 Pro. If you're already in the market for an iMac, then the 2026 Apple iMac with M6 is definitely the right choice, offering a solid improvement over the previous M4 model. The review model we tested, with 12-core processing and graphics and a larger 512GB SSD, is probably the configuration sweet spot. I'd skip the base model, which loses two Thunderbolt 4 ports, has a smaller SSD, and uses a less powerful 10-core chip. SHOULD I UPGRADE? If you're still using an old M1 iMac (or an even older Intel one), this is definitely a recommended upgrade. If you're an M4 iMac owner, meanwhile, I'd probably hold off unless you're running into bottlenecks with local performance and storage. From the laptops on your desk to satellites in space and AI that seems to be everywhere, I cover many topics at PCMag. I've covered PCs and technology products for over 15 years at PCMag and other publications, among them Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, and TWICE. As a hardware reviewer, I've handled dozens of MacBooks, 2-in-1 laptops, Chromebooks, and the latest AI PCs. As the resident Starlink expert, I've done years of hands-on testing with the satellite service. I also explore the most valuable ways to use the latest AI tools and features in our Try AI column.

item.title: REVIEW: Nocturne review: Apple TV’s thriller has a psychopath behind bars and a mystery that’ll leave you shaken
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
“Nocturne is the kind of thriller that makes you lose track of time. The mystery keeps pulling you deeper, and I would happily sacrifice a few hours of sleep to find out where it goes next.”
- An intriguing mystery with several interconnected threads - Stephen Graham delivers a quietly unsettling performance - Strong investigative tension and psychological manipulation - Effective atmosphere without relying on excessive violence - The writing occasionally makes Riverside too easy to manipulate - Karl's involvement with Jurek needs more convincing development - The mystery risks becoming overly complicated I have watched enough serial-killer thrillers and investigative dramas to know what I enjoy about the genre. From Sherlock, Mindhunter and True Detective to The Mentalist, which remains an absolute favourite, I have always been drawn to shows that make the process of solving a crime as compelling as the crime itself. There is something particularly satisfying about watching an investigator pick up on a detail everyone else has overlooked, read a suspect’s behaviour and gradually piece together a story that refuses to reveal itself all at once. I have also come to believe that this is one genre particularly suited to the OTT space. The layered investigations, character histories and steady progression of clues give these shows an inherent binge appeal, often making it difficult to stop at the end of an episode. Nocturne on Apple TV had me hooked almost immediately. I finished the premiere knowing I should probably call it a night, only to find myself fighting sleep because I wanted to watch the second episode straight away. Had Apple released the season all at once, this is exactly the kind of show I could have happily sacrificed a weekend to finish. The weekly release may eventually give the mystery room to breathe, but after two episodes, waiting for the next instalment feels more inconvenient than useful. The setup itself is familiar enough. Jurek Walter (Stephen Graham), a notorious serial killer, is already confined inside Riverside Psychiatric Hospital when Michael Frost, a boy believed to have been one of his victims, suddenly turns up alive after being missing for three years. His sister Felicia is still missing, drawing retired detective Jonah Lynn (Liev Schreiber) back towards a case that has clearly never really left him. Meanwhile, Saga Bauer (Zazie Beetz), Jonah’s protégé and surrogate daughter, decides that the only way to understand Jurek’s possible influence over events outside Riverside is to get inside the institution herself. The more intriguing part of the setup is that Jurek is already behind bars, yet the investigation suggests his influence may extend well beyond them. It gives Nocturne a compelling mystery to build on, and Stephen Graham makes for a particularly unsettling centre to it. Stephen Graham is at his unsettling best Jurek is the most compelling element of the first two episodes, and much of that comes down to how carefully the character has been constructed. Graham rarely gives him the exaggerated menace that serial-killer dramas often rely on. His voice remains measured, his body language controlled and his reactions surprisingly economical. The effect is that you begin watching the people around Jurek almost as closely as you watch him, looking for the moment when a conversation shifts and somebody realises they have given away more than they intended. The opening sequence establishes this brilliantly. Jurek is physically separated from another inmate, yet manages to communicate with him through the pipes and, within a remarkably short span of time, gets far enough inside the man’s head for him to turn violently on himself. It is a brutal scene without becoming especially graphic, and the restraint is important. The horror comes less from the violence than from understanding how little Jurek appears to have done to bring it about. His real weapon is his ability to identify what another person needs, what they fear, and how those vulnerabilities can be turned into leverage. Karl is the most immediate example. Rory Culkin gives him an underlying nervousness from the beginning, making it plausible that Jurek would recognise him as somebody who could be manipulated. The sequence involving the choking incident, another employee being implicated, and suspicion being redirected towards Karl demonstrates how quickly Jurek can work around the restrictions of a controlled environment. His line, “A truth for a truth”, is particularly revealing because it establishes the terms on which he wants every conversation to take place. I do not think Nocturne is suggesting that everything Jurek says must be a lie. The more disturbing possibility is that there is truth in much of what he reveals, but he is always the one deciding which part of it another person gets to hear. His exchanges with Jonah carry a different weight because the familiarity between them is unmistakable. Jurek appears convinced that Jonah has withheld something about the original case, while Jonah’s responses do little to suggest that the history between them is as straightforward as one man catching another. Schreiber gives Jonah the weariness of someone who has carried an investigation for far too long, but also leaves enough uncertainty around him to make his motives difficult to read. I am not yet sure how much I trust him, and that is a more interesting place for the character to be than simply presenting him as the brilliant retired detective who must be brought back because nobody else understands the killer. Graham’s performance also feels particularly interesting after Adolescence. As Eddie Miller, he played a father desperately trying to process the possibility that his teenage son had committed something horrific. Much of that performance depended on helplessness: Eddie wanted to believe his child, protect his family, and hold on to the life he understood, but events kept moving beyond his control. Jurek is almost the complete reverse. He should be the person with the least control in Nocturne, confined underground and surrounded by people whose job is to contain him, yet Graham rarely lets him feel powerless. The contrast is not simply in the characters’ circumstances; it is in the way Graham uses attention, silence, and physical restraint to make Jurek seem capable of exerting control even when everyone else believes it has been taken away from him. The wider cast is still finding its footing. Beetz gives Saga a calmer, more procedural quality than Jonah, and there is a discipline to the way she approaches an investigation once she has decided what needs to be followed. Jagannathan is another performer I was particularly interested in seeing here. I have watched her in Indian films over the years, but Nalini in Never Have I Ever remains the role I most immediately associate with her, largely because it allowed her to bring together grief, humour, protectiveness and emotional reserve without making the character feel inconsistent. As FBI investigator Quinn, she is assured and provides a useful counterpoint to Jonah’s personal history, although the first two episodes have not yet given her much that distinguishes her beyond her role in the investigation. Michael, meanwhile, is still more important as evidence than as a fully developed character. His return establishes that the original understanding of Jurek’s victims may have been wrong, introduces the possibility of Rebecca’s involvement, and gives the investigators reason to believe Felicia may still be alive. The performances give the show a strong starting point, but Graham is currently leaving the most lasting impression. Jurek’s influence may extend well beyond Riverside One of the more effective ideas in Nocturne is the discomfort of watching investigators deal with somebody whose imprisonment has not actually ended his ability to affect events outside. Jurek may be physically contained, but the series keeps finding ways to remind us that confinement and control are not necessarily the same thing. His conversations with Karl are one part of that equation; the possibility that people connected to the old case are still acting on his behalf makes the situation considerably more complicated. The dynamic immediately reminded me of Rosalind Dyer’s arc in The Rookie. Despite being incarcerated, Rosalind remained a significant threat through her influence over Caleb Wright, whose abduction of Lucy Chen turned the storyline into something much larger than simply questioning an imprisoned killer about her past crimes. The comparison is not that Jurek and Rosalind are the same kind of character. Nocturne is considerably darker and more psychologically focused. What connects them is the idea that catching a serial killer does not necessarily end the threat, particularly when the person in custody has spent years learning how to manipulate the people around them. The visit to Sally Gifford’s home in Episode 2 gives this possibility a more tangible form. Sally, a former Riverside nurse connected to Jurek, has disappeared along with her family. Jonah finds evidence suggesting they did not leave under ordinary circumstances, begins to suspect somebody is watching him, and eventually follows a figure into the woods, where he discovers a strange symbol carved into a tree. Saga later finds the same marking inside her Riverside cell. The connection is intriguing because it raises the possibility that Jurek’s influence is not limited to the individual vulnerabilities he exploits in conversation. I like that the show leaves several explanations open at this stage. The symbol could be directly connected to Jurek, belong to somebody working for him, or be used by a wider group of people. We also do not know how much Jonah understands about it, or whether his own history with the case has left him with information he has deliberately kept from the others. The series does not need to answer all of these questions immediately, but it does need to be careful about the direction it takes. Part of what makes Jurek so effective is the possibility that he does not need an elaborate network or organisation if he can persuade ordinary people to do what he wants. A larger conspiracy could add another dimension to the mystery, but it should not come at the expense of the psychological manipulation that has made him compelling so far. The show’s visual restraint supports that approach. Nocturne is not particularly interested in making every violent moment more graphic than it needs to be, and the slower camera movements through Riverside’s corridors and empty rooms help sustain an atmosphere of unease. It is not a genuinely frightening show for me so far; I would describe it as tense and unsettling rather than scary. The pleasure is investigative. You want to know what might be around the corner because it could contain another piece of information, and once Jonah begins to feel watched, even an empty section of the frame is enough to make you look twice. Saga is walking into exactly the kind of situation Jurek understands best Saga is one of the characters I am most interested in watching as the investigation develops. She is methodical, composed, and determined to maintain control over the direction of a case once she has chosen a path. Even when somebody else has a convincing argument, she does not immediately abandon what she believes needs to be followed. I feel that her decision to go undercover at Riverside is more interesting than a straightforward investigative manoeuvre. On one level, the operation makes sense. If Jurek is getting information out of the institution, somebody needs to get close enough to understand how. Saga volunteers, Quinn eventually agrees, and Jonah helps prepare her cover. The difficulty is that her reasons for wanting to get closer to Jurek are not entirely professional. Her father died by suicide after his own connection to the case, while the possibility that her missing mother, Rebecca, may also have been caught up in Jurek’s history makes the investigation deeply personal. Saga is entering Riverside believing she can stay focused, maintain her cover, and keep those experiences separate from the work, but Jurek has spent two episodes demonstrating how quickly he can identify precisely the kind of vulnerability she may be trying to conceal. The undercover setup is slightly convenient for the plot, and the series will have to work hard to justify how long Saga can realistically remain inside such a high-risk environment without Jurek recognising what she is doing. However, the dramatic possibilities are strong. The investigators have spent the opening episodes showing us how Jurek gets inside people’s heads, and now they have placed somebody with an enormous personal stake in the case directly within his reach. I want the operation to test Saga’s judgement and investigative instincts, rather than relying only on the physical danger of being close to him. Nocturne has more than one mystery to solve The premiere is easily the stronger of the two episodes in terms of execution, performance, and momentum. Part of that comes from how much information it introduces without making the investigation feel static. Michael has returned, Felicia remains missing, Jonah is pulled back towards a case he clearly never escaped emotionally, Jurek appears capable of influencing people from confinement, and Saga has her own connection to the history surrounding the investigation. The FBI’s arrival adds another perspective to a case that local law enforcement may not have handled as cleanly as everyone wants to believe. There is a slight overload to the premiere, but I enjoyed that feeling because it makes the investigation immediately active. You spend much of the episode trying to understand where all these people fit and what their roles might eventually become. Episode 2 has a different job to do. It needs to begin organising those pieces, provide more context for the relationships and establish how the renewed investigation might connect to events that happened years earlier. Jonah’s history with Saga’s father becomes more important, Rebecca potentially enters the larger mystery when Michael refers to a woman called Becca who may have protected him and Felicia, and Jurek’s connection to the original investigation becomes messier. The police also begin confronting the possibility that the case they believed they had solved may not have been solved at all. Some of the premiere’s urgency inevitably falls away as the series starts putting these threads in place, but the second episode leaves the story in a wider and, in some ways, more intriguing position than it found it. I would not call the pacing a problem yet. A mystery of this scale needs time to establish the relationships and the history behind the case, particularly when so many characters appear to be withholding information. The question is whether the series can make those connections feel earned as it moves forward, rather than relying on a steady supply of new clues to keep the investigation moving. Riverside sometimes makes Jurek’s life too easy My biggest reservation after two episodes is the way the writing occasionally makes the people and systems surrounding Jurek a little too convenient. The Karl storyline is where I felt this most strongly. The choking incident, the vomiting, the planting of evidence, and the suspicion being redirected towards another employee all happen with considerable efficiency. I understand what the sequence is trying to establish: Jurek can read a situation quickly, improvise, and protect the person he needs. However, Riverside is also supposed to be the institution designed to contain an exceptionally dangerous and psychologically sophisticated serial killer. If Jurek repeatedly succeeds because the people around him are surprisingly easy to fool, the show risks weakening the very intelligence it wants us to recognise in him. I want to watch him outthink capable people and strong systems, rather than benefit from convenient gaps in their judgement. Karl’s continued cooperation could also use more development. I understand why Jurek sees him as vulnerable, but the speed with which that vulnerability turns into sustained involvement needs more convincing groundwork, particularly when the consequences of getting involved should be difficult to ignore. Nocturne is really about who thinks they are in control Underneath the serial-killer investigation, Nocturne is already developing a more interesting question about control. The institution believes it controls Jurek because he is physically contained. Karl may believe he can simply stop helping him, Jonah trusts his experience with the case, and Saga believes she can enter Riverside with a cover identity and keep her personal history out of the investigation. Quinn brings the confidence of procedure to a situation that is already complicated by old loyalties and unanswered questions. Jurek, meanwhile, seems interested in testing every one of those assumptions. His lack of obvious aggression is central to why the premise works. He does not need to prove he is stronger than the people around him. He needs them to believe they are making their own decisions while quietly changing the conditions under which those decisions are made. The investigators may be trained, experienced and backed by an entire institution, but none of that necessarily means they understand the person they are trying to contain. Their confidence in their own ability to handle him could eventually become as important as Jurek’s talent for manipulation. The first episode is the stronger introduction, but the second leaves the story in a more intriguing place. Saga is inside Riverside, Jonah has found a symbol that appears there too, Sally Gifford and her family are missing, Michael has introduced the possibility that Rebecca is connected to everything, and Felicia remains unaccounted for. There is enough material here to sustain the mystery without the show having to keep adding twists simply to make the story bigger. What I want now is for it to deepen the relationships, make Karl’s vulnerability more convincing, give Quinn a clearer identity within the investigation, and reveal what Jonah has been holding back. Most of all, I want to understand how much of what is happening outside Riverside Jurek is actually controlling. The show has established that he is dangerous and that he understands people exceptionally well; the more consequential question is whether the investigators understand the difference between locking a psychopath inside a room and taking away his power. Two episodes in, I am not convinced they do, and if Episode 3 were sitting there after I finished the second one, I would happily give up a few more hours of sleep to find out. Nocturne is now streaming on Apple TV.

item.title: REVIEW: Apple Unveils 2026 iPad mini with OLED Display and Waterproof Design
item.description:
Source: PCMag, Ars Technica
Apple has released the 2026 iPad mini, marking a significant upgrade from its 2024 predecessor with a major leap in display technology, performance, and durability. The new model features an OLED screen replacing the previous LCD display, a transition that enhances brightness and color accuracy. The device also introduces the A20 Pro chip, a substantial upgrade from the A17 Pro, offering improved processing power and efficiency. Additionally, the 2026 iPad mini becomes the first waterproof iPad with an IP67 rating, providing dust and water resistance—a notable addition for users seeking greater durability. These advancements come at a cost: the 2026 model starts at $699 for the 128GB version, a $100 increase from the 2024 model’s $599 price point. The 256GB variant is $799, and the 512GB model reaches $999, with an additional $150 for 5G connectivity. At $1,149 for the highest configuration, the new iPad mini now costs more than some MacBook Air models, raising questions about its value proposition. Ars Technica noted that the 2026 iPad mini’s screen is 0.2 inches larger than its predecessor, offering a more immersive experience for media and multitasking. The device’s dimensions have also been refined, shrinking to 7.69 by 5.22 by 0.21 inches and reducing weight to 0.56 pounds, making it lighter than the 2024 model. Despite these improvements, the 2026 iPad mini retains the same button placement and USB-C port as before. PCMag highlighted that the new model sacrifices color options, now available only in Midnight (black) or Starlight (gold), whereas the 2024 version offered a broader range of colors. The removal of speaker grilles on the short edges contributes to the IP67 rating, though the overall design remains largely unchanged. While the 2026 iPad mini represents a significant step forward in performance and durability, its higher price point and limited color options may deter some buyers. The device’s waterproof feature and improved display make it a stronger contender for users prioritizing portability and resilience, but its value proposition remains a key consideration for potential purchasers.

Make quick and easy work of fertilizer, driveway salt, and more with the Ryobi power spreader. Ryobi 18V Outdoor Patio Cleaner and Sweeper I hate sweeping out my garage and cleaning up my backyard patio when it gets messy. Ditch the broom and use this instead, plus it's a little more gentle and controllable than a leaf blower for certain situations. The Ryobi cordless 18V sweeper brush makes it easy to clean a dirty garage, patio, decking, and so much more. Ryobi Hybrid Battery-Powered 24qt. Cooler Another neat Ryobi product that you probably didn't know about is its battery-powered iceless cooler. This came out a few years back, was rarely in stock, and most people don't know it exists. item.title: REVIEW: JMGO N3 Ultimate review: this projector is so, so bright, but less compelling at night
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Extreme brightness and tons of flexibility at a competitive price make the JMGO N3 Ultimate a great option for anyone who doesn’t plan on creating a near-black home theater environment. - +Optical and gimbal make for quick or clear adjustments - -Elevated black levels harm dark scenes Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The JMGO N3 Ultimate is the new, top-of-the-line option from JMGO. It brings a lot of what the brand had already been packing into a new design with a motorized gimbal stand and adjustable optics that provide quick or finely controlled setup options. The JMGO N3 Ultimate's projection can be splendid, thanks to bright RGB lasers that give the projector enough juice to hold up in even well-lit rooms. The N3 Ultimate has vivid color and crisp detail, too. Unfortunately, the brightness isn’t matched by effective dimming to offer better performance in dark scenes, which is perhaps its biggest setback. Its motion could also be smoother without so many artifacts, but it’s not terrible either. All told, it’s a capable projector that could serve a lot of people well, as long as they’re not seeking out dark, home theater setups where contrast is as important as brightness. At its $2,999 / £2,499 list price, it’s competitively priced compared to the best projectors, but it’s been on sale for much less and becomes all the better a bargain. JMGO N3 Ultimate Review: Price and release date The JMGO N3 Ultimate launched in 2026 and is now widely available. It has a $2,999 £2,499 list price, but it has already seen substantial discounts. At the time of writing, it was available for $2,349 / £2,119. JMGO N3 Ultimate Review: Design and features - Motorized gimbal stand and optical lens adjustments JMGO has been rocking the same design for a few years now, and the JMGO N3 Ultimate does little to shift that. It’s still a fairly compact, two-tone rounded box sitting aloft on a gimbal stand with a rotating base, making it easy to set up and point the projection where you want it. This go around, JMGO has incorporated small motors for electronic control of the stand. By holding a dedicated button on the remote control and using gyro controls, you can adjust the tilt and rotation of the projector. It’s good for quick adjustment but not for fine tuning. In an interesting twist, the N3 Ultimate is JMGO’s projector that least needed this technology, as the projector incorporates advanced optics with adjustable zoom and lens shift. The zoom can shift the projector from a 0.88:1 to a 1.7:1 throw ratio, giving it a ton of range. Meanwhile, the lens shift lets it move the projection up or down by 130% or sideways by 53%, so you really just need to point it perpendicular to your wall, and you should have no trouble shifting and squeezing the projection to fit without any keystone correction. Those manual controls are how you’ll get the best picture, but the JMGO N3 Ultimate has a host of automated tools that can quickly make adjustments for you, which may be convenient if you’re moving it often. It can analyze the projection area available to it, re-aiming, shrinking, and shifting the picture to fit. I found this using digital keystone even when it really wasn’t called for, though, so I wouldn’t count on it doing the best job. One additional automatic tool that may be more helpful is the wall color adaptation. This uses the projector's camera and a series of test patterns to tweak colors so they appear better on your wall. You won’t need this if you use a screen, but it worked well on my beige walls. Since the projector can move quite a bit in operation, it fits its connectors all at the base, rather than the rear of the projection unit itself. This can still get in the way of rotation, but makes vertical tilt a non-issue. The projector doesn’t have a great selection of ports, though, with just two HDMI 2.1 ports, one of which is eARC and probably should be kept for that purpose. There’s also a single USB-A port. Thankfully, you don’t need to use any of those HDMI ports for basic streaming. The projector has built-in Google TV, and it operates quickly on its 4GB of memory. Annoyingly, it pauses playback while navigating menus sometimes (sometimes it doesn’t), but it’s quite serviceable otherwise. It even gets 64GB of storage, which can be useful if you use lots of apps. Perhaps, more crucially, the projector connects over Wi-Fi 6, giving it faster and more stable connectivity to work with while streaming. For cinephiles, the JMGO N3 Ultimate supports HDR10 and Dolby Vision. Meanwhile, for gamers the projector can shift from 4K60Hz over to 1080p/240Hz and even brings VRR for smooth, low-latency, responsive gaming. There are some trade-offs though. Enabling VRR hurt clarity no matter if I left the projector at 4K or swapped to 1080p. Even at 1080p, VRR took a small toll on clarity. Fine text exhibited artifacts that looked like chroma subsampling. In games, it wasn’t an issue, but navigating Windows on PC to select games to play, it was a nuisance. Apart from its gyro controls, the Ultimate's remote is pretty basic. It has the standard Google TV controls and thankfully a pill-shaped volume control that’s easy to feel out in the dark. It includes shortcuts to Prime Video, Netflix, YouTube, and one app of your choice. Google TV Freeplay gets a separate shortcut at the top of the remote. Annoyingly, there’s no mute button for quick silencing and while the remote has motion-activated lighting behind some of its keys, it doesn't behind the shortcut buttons. Since the JMGO N3 Ultimate is fairly portable, JGMO includes a foam carrying case that can fit it, the remote, and the power adapter all inside. It’s not exceedingly robust or impressive, but it’s not too bulky and should do a better job protecting the hardware than a typical backpack would. JMGO N3 Ultimate Review: Picture quality and performance - Crisp 4K visuals and responsive 1080p gaming The JMGO N3 Ultimate has brightness in spades, and that’s where it shines best. When it comes to darkness, it can struggle. It fails to sink into darkness where it needs to, and the raised grays are distracting to see, never mind the regularly present letterboxes. Even when scenes aren’t very dark, these shortcomings are clear. Neither Dolby Vision nor adaptive brightness features seem to do the trick. Thankfully, as soon as more light is called for, the JMGO N3 Ultimate delivers. It pumped out over 5,200 lumens by my measurements, which is plenty for most scenarios and not too far off the rated 5,800 lumens (nor did it require an awful picture setting). Bright scenes are clear and vibrant. Shadows look stronger in contrast to the brightness and the brightness is even enough to give the JMGO N3 Ultimate a solid showing in a modestly lit room. This makes it a great match for casual viewing, news, and bright cartoons. That brightness makes it all the easier to go big without the image getting too dim. Alongside the brightness, the color of the RGB laser projection is stunning, just as it’s been in other projectors I’ve tested with the tech. When watching Supergirl, the glow of the green sun has plenty of depth, and the red cape glows majestically whenever the sun hits it. When Kara’s laser vision rips through the Brigands, it’s properly dazzling. The world of Pandora in the Avatar series is also lushly presented. Motion can be hit or miss. By default the projector wants to use unsightly interpolation that presents loads of artifacts and makes the projection feel like anything but high-fidelity. With the MEMC setting dropped to low, it doesn’t look so bad, avoiding distracting soap opera effect and serious artifacts while helping reduce some of the stutter that occurs when it’s disabled entirely. One area RGB laser projectors have been improving is the DLP rainbow effect. I’m not terribly sensitive to it, but I can usually catch it if I’m looking for it. Lately, I’ve been spotting it less and less on high-end laser projectors, but I can still catch it on the JMGO N3 Ultimate. Thankfully, it’s subtle, and I find it’s largely limited to subtitles The adjustable optics help ensure a sharp picture from wherever you want to project. Stretched across about an 150-inch section of my wall, 4K looked brilliant in my living room. Outside of movies, the JMGO N3 Ultimate proves a great option for gaming. You want crisp detail from corner to corner in games, since you never know where something precious is hiding, and the optics help provide this. Latency is satisfyingly low at 4K but sinks to negligible levels at 1080p/240Hz. Mousing around my screen and zipping through levels in Hades 2, I didn’t feel a hint of latency in that mode. The speakers on the JMGO N3 Ultimate aren’t bad, but they certainly aren’t an adequate match for the projection. They put out decent volume, helping ensure you’ve got enough sound to work with when you want to plop the projector down somewhere and start enjoying right away. They even provide some low-end, helping bump up effects in movies. But the quality of stereo sound won’t be very good unless you’re sitting perfectly in center with the projection. - Picture quality & performance score: 3.5 / 5 - Cheaper than many rivals while offering competitive brightness The JGMO N3 Ultimate is a capable projector and can work well for folks who aren’t committing to a pitch-black home theater where its weaker black levels will steal focus. At $2,999 / £2,499, it’s still fairly competitive with what’s on the market, but at $2,349 / £2,119, it’s more of a steal. It can compete with large TVs on value while providing the flexibility to enjoy movies and TV in 4K or switch over to 1080p for high-speed gaming. The different realms it can cover all from a single product help boost its value. Should I buy the JMGO N3 Ultimate? Buy it if... You don’t like turning out all the lights The JMGO N3 Ultimate has brightness to spare, letting it handle dim and even well-lit rooms fairly well. If you don’t like viewing in the dark, this makes it a good match. The JMGO N3 can work in a lot of different setups and it makes getting it all lined up easy. If you’re always moving your projector around, that can save you a load of time. The JGMO N3 Ultimate can tackle 4K video, 1080p gaming, precise and careful optical setup, or quick and effortless setup. Its ability to step into different roles can be very convenient if you have a lot of different needs. Don't buy it if... Few projectors do a great job with their black levels, and even the best aren’t really on the level with OLEDs. The JMGO N3 Ultimate isn’t even close, with raised black levels that don’t really look great in dark scenes. With just two HDMI ports, the JMGO N3 Ultimate is a recipe for annoyance if you have a handful of consoles, a Blu-ray player and the like. Heck, it doesn’t even have a 3.5mm jack you can use to free up the eARC port. A big part of the package, and therefore what you pay for, is the flexibility of the gimbal and optics. If you’re not planning to take advantage of them, you can save some money by looking elsewhere. This projector may not be as bright, but it has wonderfully flexible optics, great visual performance and profound black levels that make it a far more worthy home theater projector. It tends to be a bit more expensive, though. The Hisense C2 Ultra isn’t nearly as bright and doesn’t have the same degree of flexible optics as the JMGO N3 Ultimate. Still, it tends to cost nearly as much. This helps highlight how much the technology has progressed and come down in price in a short time. Read our full Hisense C2 Ultra review. This model has most of the same capabilities and qualities as the JGMO N3 Ultimate, just in a different package. It had strong contrast in our testing, but it skips the motorized gimbal. If you know you want that dark performance, it’ll probably be the better pick, though you may be best just grabbing whichever is cheapest when you’re shopping since both have frequent discounts. Read our full Xgimi Horizon 20 Max review. - Tested at home in multiple, real-world viewing conditions - Presented the display with a variety of media and formats - I have tested numerous projectors and displays over the last half-decade I tested the JMGO N3 Ultimate at home, in real-world conditions. This saw it faced with ambient light coming in from numerous windows, in-room lighting, as well as ambient noise that both the projector and speaker systems had to overcome. The projector was tested both against a bare, white wall and an Akia Screens CineWhite screen. It was presented with streamed content, HDR and non-HDR, and console gameplay. My testing evaluates the projector’s performance with respect to its price and competition from other models I and colleagues at TechRadar have tested. I have been testing projectors since 2021 and displays for even longer.

item.title: SALES: Best Platforms That Help Tech Companies Build Media Coverage and AI Visibility
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
Best Platforms That Help Tech Companies Build Media Coverage and AI Visibility The five platforms below help tech companies get covered in the publicatio eir future customers read, from self-service placement marketplaces to managed publisher outreach. They were chosen for how well they serve tech brands that want both media ns th presence and a footprint AI assistants can draw on. The table matches each one to the kind of team and campaign it suits best. The platforms for tech media coverage at a glance Media coverage wins tech buyers months before they start shopping Most potential customers aren’t looking for a product when they first come across a company. Research by Professor John Dawes of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, published with LinkedIn’s B2B Institute, found that only about 5% of B2B buyers are in-market at any given time, while the other 95% may not buy for months or even years. When the need arises, the brands buyers already recognize start with an advantage. The same coverage feeds AI assistants. An Ahrefs study of 75,000 brands found that branded web mentions correlate strongly with how often a brand appears in ChatGPT, AI Mode, and AI Overviews, at 0.66 to 0.71, well above link and content volume. The difficulty for tech companies is finding the right publications and staying present in them without spending all their time on coordination. The platforms below handle that work in different ways, depending on the target market, the team’s resources, and the type of coverage it wants. Medialister is an AdTech platform for planning, buying, and managing paid media placements in outlets across 176 countries. A campaign starts from a goal such as AI visibility, product awareness, or entering a new market, and the platform answers with tailored filters and ready-made media selections for it. After free registration, each outlet’s Similarweb, Ahrefs, and Semrush metrics sit next to its publishing terms and final price. Teams that already have a list of target outlets, such as publications where competitors appear, can upload up to 5,000 domains or URLs to the Bulk Media Search tool and see which of them are available to book in the catalog. A free MCP server turns Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini CLI into a workspace for the whole campaign: the assistant shortlists outlets that AI systems frequently cite as sources, prepares content to each outlet’s rules, and tracks placements through to publication, while a person approves every payment. - Formats: articles, press releases, interviews, thought leadership, listicles, mentions - Pricing: pay per placement plus a fixed commission; post-payment for agencies PRNEWS is a platform for buying and managing paid media placements in almost 175 countries, 77 languages, and 37 content categories, including business, technology, and finance. Publishers pass identity or company verification before listing, and buyers see each outlet’s price, publishing terms, Ahrefs DR, and Semrush Authority Score before ordering. Content writing and translation into the local language can be added to an order, which helps when one campaign runs in several markets. Agencies and in-house teams running several clients or campaigns can keep separate projects, manage a team, and give guest access to colleagues or clients. For teams planning coverage at scale, the PRO account includes tools such as the Bulk Site Checker. It can compare a list of domains, including outlets where competitors already appear, with the PRNEWS catalog and return prices and metrics for hundreds of sites at once. - Pricing: pay per placement; optional PRO subscription INSERT.LINK is a self-service marketplace built around page-level search rather than domain lists. A user enters a target keyword, and NLP-powered search returns already published, indexed articles on that topic from more than 50 million pages, so a tech company can find pieces about its software category, a use case, or the problem its product solves. Page traffic, keywords, and topical relevance are visible for each result before ordering. Buyers review each publisher, page, set of metrics, and price themselves before placing an order. Coverage spans 152 locations, and a separate list of Fast Delivery Sites groups publishers with quicker turnaround, where some placements go live within three days. An MCP server and API connect the marketplace to a team’s own tools. - Formats: in-content mentions, guest posts, listicle placements, press releases - Pricing: pay-as-you-go, from $20–25 per placement - Turnaround: up to 3 days on Fast Delivery Sites; otherwise not disclosed Respona works through outreach rather than a catalog: its done-for-you service finds relevant publications and secures brand mentions in them on a client’s behalf. The client sets target pages, a quality bar, and optional AI prompts to monitor, and the team handles prospecting, outreach, follow-ups, negotiation, content, and publication, with placement status and AI visibility tracked in one dashboard. By default the team chooses the domains, and approving each one in advance is a paid add-on. Teams that would rather pitch editors themselves get a separate DIY platform that finds editors’ personal email addresses, personalizes pitches with AI based on their past articles, and sends follow-up sequences automatically. - Model: managed service + outreach tool - Catalog: not available (no catalog) - Formats: listicles, product reviews, comparisons, guest posts, editorial mentions - Pricing: pay per result, 100–500 per placement depending on publisher tier; DIY tool by subscription from $198 a month - Turnaround: 28 days per placement as standard; 14 days with paid expedited delivery Linksman is a self-service marketplace and outreach service for SaaS companies, agencies, and marketers, with publishers across 15+ niches, from SaaS and technology to business, finance, and marketing. Every site is reviewed manually and checked for real ownership before it is listed. The distinctive format is SaaS outreach, where the team manually finds relevant IT and business publications and works a product into expert reviews, software comparisons, and analytical pieces. For mentions in content that already exists, a Link Suggestion Tool finds published articles that match target keywords. - Formats: guest posts, in-content mentions, listicle placements, SaaS outreach - Pricing: per order or ready-made packages, from $50 per placement A tech brand earns lasting visibility when it gives the media a reason to talk about it These platforms help tech companies reach the publications their future customers read and build a broader footprint across the web. Visibility still depends on what a company brings to the conversation: a product that solves a clear problem, original research, a useful comparison, or an expert perspective. Those details give editors a reason to cover the company and give AI assistants concrete information to draw on when people ask about its products. Start with the audience you want to reach and the publications it already trusts. A marketplace suits teams that want to pick and buy placements themselves, page-level search suits cases where the right article already exists, and managed outreach suits teams that need help building publisher relationships. A paid article, a mention in existing content, and editorial coverage earned through outreach give different levels of control over the result, so many teams combine two routes to stay present in the sources that shape buyer awareness.

item.title: SALES: Perplexity’s new AI coworkers can take over your workload, but they don’t come cheap
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
I’d happily hand off half my to-do list if the helper didn’t need to be re-explained every morning. Well, it looks like Perplexity thinks it has built that helper. Perplexity launched Teammates on Thursday. It basically refers to the personal AI agents that take on ongoing work from a high-level goal. They’ll be available first to Max subscribers on the web (via Perplexity). What can Perplexity Teammates actually do? Back in February, Perplexity launched Computer, its multi-model agent (also for its Max tier). I ran in temporary sandbox sessions or workspaces that vanished after each job. Teammates, by contrast, stick around. CEO Aravind Srinivas calls them persistent coworkers that take over responsibilities and get tasks done end to end. They already have all the content about your Projects, Memory, Skills, connectors, files, and past sessions. Perplexity’s examples span a variety of use cases, including those in marketing, sales, support, and operations. For instance, Teammates can triage bugs, run QA loops, monitor security, analyze data, and even manage A/B tests. Unlike some humans, Teammates can also learn from their mistakes and feedback. In the demo, an ads teammate spots creator ads beating the customer acquisition cost target, preps a bigger campaign, and sends its contract extension to the legal team. The brand director says to do that every time without asking next time. Who can use Teammates, and who else is chasing this? If you add a teammate to a chaHow to use Slacknnel in Slack, coworkers can hand it work, while it watches the channel and acts when something changes (the way it’s programmed). Each runs in its own environment, and you can review its work, take over its desktop, or redirect it. Beyond the web, Teammates are also coming to iOS. Srinivas says native mobile and desktop apps are coming. Free and Pro users must upgrade to Max, though, which costs $200 per month. None of this is happening in a vacuum, though. OpenAI’s workspace agents, Microsoft’s Copilot Cowork, Grok Bot, and Anthropic’s Claude Cowork are already chasing the same idea, though the first two target organizations rather than individual subscribers.
